newsitem.title: USA: Second NY bar panel eyes "pay-to-play" curbs.
newsitem.headline: Second NY bar panel eyes "pay-to-play" curbs.

text.p: A new powerful lawyers' group is moving toward recommending curbs on "pay-to-play" by attorneys with municipal market clients, an informed source said on Tuesday.

The ethics committee of the New York State Bar Association tentatively voted 12 to 2 at a meeting last week to support, in principle, a resolution proposed recently by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York on the controversial issue, the source said.
The resolution would prohibit muni lawyers that solicit or make political contributions to municipal clients from engaging in bond business for two years with those governments.
The rule is partly modeled after a standard adopted by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board in 1994 for muni bond dealers, although it is more restrictive.
An official with the New York State bar association would not comment on the action by the group's ethics committee.

It would be "premature" to comment, the official, Richard Ziegler, told Reuters by telephone. Ziegler, a partner with Cleary, Gottlieb, Steen & Hamilton in New York City, chairs the group's professional ethics committee.
He confirmed, however, that his panel has been asked by state bar association leaders to review the City bar's initiative.
William Josephson, who chaired the City bar panel that developed the proposal, was pleased with the state bar's preliminary action.
"I think it's extremely welcome news," said Josephson, a partner with Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson in New York City.
"The state bar is the statewide professional organization of all the New York lawyers. It will have a very positive impact on the Administrative Board," he said.

Josephson was referring to the New York State Administrative Board, which sets standards for the state's thousands of lawyers. The City bar group has asked the panel to adopt the rule for all lawyers in the state.
The board this spring asked staff to draft a rule for its further consideration on the issue.
